caption: aludol.com
copy:
I teach at a private school that costs $15,000 a year. Last Thursday, I asked my 6th graders one question: If the Earth spins at 1,000 miles per hour, why don't we fly off? Twenty-three students. Not a single real answer. Their parents are paying for brilliance. We're delivering polished memorization.

I've been teaching for eleven years.

The families at this school are driven. They write a $15,000 check every year because they want their children to be exceptional. They want them to be the sharpest minds in any room.

Last Thursday, I tried something I'd never attempted. A Thinking Quiz. No grades. No right or wrong. Just three questions.

Why is the ocean blue when the water in your glass is clear?

If you're on a spinning planet, why don't you feel it?

Why does the moon seem to chase your car at night?

I watched 23 sixth-graders sit there in silence.

A few of them scribbled down vocabulary words they'd memorized from a textbook. But none of them could actually explain the logic.

Ten minutes later, I picked up the papers.

Lily: "It just is that way."

James: "Gravity???" with three question marks.

Ava: "Because God designed it like that."

Noah: Left his paper completely empty.

These are straight-A kids.

Principal's list.

Already taking pre-algebra.

And not one of them could reason through a basic question for half a minute.

I sat in my classroom during lunch staring at those papers and felt nauseous. These families are spending $15,000 a year. They believe we're building powerful thinkers.

We're not.

We're teaching kids to pass exams. We're producing a generation of children who can look up anything on Google but can't work through a problem on their own for five minutes.

That evening at dinner, I couldn't get those empty papers out of my head.

I looked across the table at my daughter, Mia. She's 10. Six years at this academy. $90,000 in tuition so far.

"Mia, quick one. Why is the sky blue and not purple?"

She glanced up from her tablet. "Light …
description: Aludol
